newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jewish minister says Switzerland fears own past.
newsitem.headline: Jewish minister says Switzerland fears own past.

text.p: Switzerland's only Jewish government minister said on Sunday the country had a fear of facing its own World War Two role and should work to bring relief to those who had suffered from the Holocaust.

Speaking on French-language television, Interior Minister Ruth Dreifuss also said recent remarks by a senior cabinet colleague had undermined confidence abroad that Berne would move to compensate Jews whose money disappeared in Swiss banks.
"We have a fear of our own past and what could emerge...Nothing is more difficult than one's own past and the image one has of onseself and breaking an image one has of onseself," she told viewers.
"Just as an individual person needs a psychiatrist to find his way, we need to be confronted with the truth that is being dug up now," she declared.

Her intervention, which followed an interview published earlier in the day with a Zurich German-language newspaper, marked the first time she had spoken out over the problem centring on the fate of money left by Holocaust victims in Swiss banks and how Switzerland treated wartime Jewish refugees.
In the interview with SonntagsZeitung, Dreifuss said the Federal Council or cabinet was aware of the need to move swiftly on compensating Jews or their descendants whose deposits had disappeared.
"It is quite clear to the council that something has to be done fast," she said.

The cabinet was not planning to renounce remarks by economics minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, who while still holding the country's rotating presidency at the end of last month had described calls for a quick Swiss restitution to Holocaust victims as blackmail.
"Normally the council as a collective group does not correct statements made by individual members," Dreifuss said, noting such a move was not part of the country's political custom.
Most Swiss seem to agree the government should not denounce Delamuraz, nor should he resign, according to polls published at the weekend.

A survey by the Lucerne-based LINK institute, published by the Blick tabloid on Saturday, showed that less than one-third of the Swiss surveyed thought the government should distance itself from Delamuraz.
Another survey, by the Sunday SonntagsBlick, showed that 80 percent of respondents did not think Delamuraz should resign, while 10 percent called for his resignation.
In her newspaper interview, Dreifuss said she regretted that Delamuraz' remarks had undermined the confidence and trust that had been built up between Switzerland and Jewish groups abroad.
Delamuraz' remarks angered Israeli politicians and world Jewish organisations, who are threatening to call on Jews around the world to pull their funds out of Swiss banks.
On Friday Swiss President Arnold Koller also made clear the government did not plan to apologise for Delamuraz' remarks.

Dreifuss told Sonntagszeitung that other countries -- like Sweden, Hungary, Portugal and even France -- were now having to look more closely at how they behaved towards Hitler's Jewish victims, but said some had already set up funds.

"We are also ready to take action," she said. In her television interivew, she said she knew that many Swiss had done their best to help Jews and many had joined the anti-Nazi resistance in neighbouring countries.
